#242. ‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling

Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world

There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.

For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.

By the time they spilled into the court’s halls, the relief was evident. A Rohingya community leader threw a big thumbs up as he left the courtroom and others immediately took out their phones to call family in the refugee camps.

Salma, 30, a Rohingya survivor who lost family members in the 2017 genocide, said: “Everyone worked hard and struggled for this justice, for this cause. When they hear it today, everyone will be happy, thank God. I don’t know how to express it or even what to do with myself.”

Another Rohingya present, who cannot be named because of safety concerns, said they cried as the judge went through each of the rulings.

“During the last few minutes I couldn’t even sit down any more, I had to move to the back because I didn’t know how I’d react,” they said. “I saw some of the other Rohingya around me crying. They were so emotional.

“Now the responsibility is with the international governments. It has been declared genocide now and they have to act.”

In Bangladesh, where most of the Rohingya population have lived – in the world’s largest refugee camp – since being forced to flee in 2017, the verdict was translated into the Rohingya language for the crowds who had gathered to watch on screens specially set up for the purpose.

They immediately leapt up, cheering, applauding and shouting gratitude for the Gambia – the faraway African nation that brought the case to the ICJ on behalf of the stateless minority. Many held posters that read “Thank You Gambia” and “Justice = Safe Return”.

“Since we arrived here, we have been waiting and looking forward to this justice,” said Farida Khatun, 50, who has been a refugee in Bangladesh since 2017, when her village, Tula Toli, was targeted by soldiers. The village in north-western Myanmar, near the Bangladesh border, was the scene of a massacre in August of that year, with reports of mass killings and gang rapes.

She said, however, that she does not expect to be able to return home. Tula Toli was completely destroyed by Myanmar’s forces and no longer exists. “Even though today’s verdict makes us happy, my heart still cannot believe that they will take us back in true peace.”

The case has taken seven years to reach this point, with Rohingya researchers working to collect testimony from survivors. The initial hope for justice had faded during the long wait for a ruling. Many were also left deflated during early hearings when the one-time pro-democracy hero Aung San Suu Kyi defended the Myanmar military at The Hague.

Before today’s ruling, some were optimistic, others were prepared to be disappointed, but all said they knew themselves that they were victims of genocide.

The tension was finally released when the court declared Myanmar was responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, highlighting the use of sexual violence and attacks on children alongside the killing of Rohingya who tried to flee violence, which it said meant the violence amounted to more than ethnic cleansing.

The court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations for the Rohingya and end continuing breaches of the genocide convention.

There is now also an international criminal court investigation into the violence of 2017, looking specifically at the crime of mass deportation, and for which prosecutors in 2024 sought an arrest warrant for Myanmar’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing.

With continuing violence against the Rohingya, the possibility of a return to Myanmar, as happened after previous exoduses to Bangladesh in 1978 and the early 1990s, remains unlikely.

But many hope the ICJ ruling will be the start of a process of ensuring justice and lead to real international pressure to ensure their safety in Myanmar.

“We will be able to return to our homeland – with our rights, with our citizenship, and having received our full security. We will be able to return,” says Salma.

Last but not least, you can also buy the Sonos Ace for $229 ($120 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and directly from Sonos, which marks a new low price. The newer Ace Ultra offer better sound and improved noise cancellation, but the Ace is still a solid option, especially if you already own a Sonos soundbar. Unlike the newer Ultra, though, they can’t transfer music from your other Sonos speakers to your headphones. However, their TV Audio Swap feature still lets you transfer audio from a compatible Sonos soundbar to your headphones, so you can watch movies or listen to music playing on your TV without disturbing anyone else.

#239. What pet cemeteries reveal about being human

Editor’s Note:  Eric Tourigny is a lecturer in historical archaeology at Newcastle University, UK. His research interprets osteological and material culture remains alongside historic texts to examine changing human-animal relationships in Europe and North America over the past 500 years. The views expressed in this commentary are his own. Read more opinion on CNN.

Why do we bury our departed loved ones in a cemetery? A primary purpose is to provide survivors with an opportunity to grieve and gain a sense of closure. The cemetery is a place for the living as much as it is a place for the dead.

But what about when the dearly departed are not human – but our pets?

The Spanish city of Barcelona recently announced that it will be investing in the establishment of the country’s first public pet cemetery. Set to open next year, it will offer both burials and cremations – with an estimated 7,000 carried out each year.

For me, as someone who has spent years researching the development of pet cemeteries elsewhere in the world, this news came as a shock. Barcelona is a densely populated city with limited privately owned land – one where 50% of families own a pet.

How did a city that is home to 180,000 dogs not already have a public pet cemetery? Until now, the service was only provided by the private sector, according to Barcelona’s Councilor for Climate Emergency and Ecological Transition, Eloi Badia. He added that the municipal-funded initiative was sparked by “constant public demand.”

After all, public pet cemeteries have been around in Europe and the Americas since the late 19th century. Britain’s first public pet cemetery appeared in London’s Hyde Park in 1881. New York’s Hartsdale pet cemetery was founded in 1896, followed a few years later by Paris’ ornate Cimetière des Chiens in 1899.

I became interested in the history of modern pet burial practices while investigating the archaeological record of a centuries-old house in Toronto. I came across a (very) large dog buried in the back garden which, according to the historical record, was occupied between 1840 and 1870.

This dog survived to an elderly age but, sadly, suffered from degenerative joint disease and severe infections during his last months. His ailments progressed to such a state that suggest he received some level of care in his final weeks. He then was buried in a personal plot behind the family home.

This elderly dog led me to think about the different ways people interact with the bodies of their pets after death. Could this behavior be reflective of the relationships they held with their animals in life? In this instance, why take the time to carefully bury a dog in its own space when other, arguably easier options existed?

This, after all, was an era when people often disposed of their dead pets in the river, or might have sold their bodies for meat and skin.

Good hygiene is an obvious reason to choose a burial – no one wants decomposing animal bodies in the street or their garden – but that wouldn’t immediately warrant a personalized, dedicated burial and gravestone.

The most straight forward option would be to dispose of a deceased animal with the household waste. But such treatment would evidently feel less ceremonious and would not offer appropriate emotional closure to what was likely an important relationship.

Like the burial of people, the burial of pets is an intimate cultural practice, one that changes over time and is reflective of the changing relationships that a society has with its cherished creatures.

My study of historic gravestones and epitaphs in Britain from the Victorian period to today shows this changing human-animal relationship. In the 19th century, gravestones were often dedicated to a “loving friend” or “devoted companion,” suggesting pets were mostly considered important friends.

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

Society’s changing attitude towards the role of animals in the afterlife can also be found. Fast-forward a few decades later, and gravestones were more likely to reference a reunion then earlier ones. For example, the owners of Denny, the “brave little cat” buried in an east London cemetery in 1952, wrote on his epitaph “God bless until we meet again.”

I wonder what the epitaphs in Barcelona’s new cemetery will reveal about modern Catalan relationships with animals.

Over time, our ways of treating our animal dead appear to reflect an even closer relationship in life. Once strictly forbidden by law, the last decade saw many jurisdictions, like the state of New York, allowing the co-burial of cremated animals and people, which will undoubtedly lead to changing funerary and commemoration practices for both humans and animals.

For me, the most remarkable similarity between modern and historic pet cemeteries is the striking evidence for the heartbreak and taboos around grieving for animals.

The connection that someone has with their pet can be just as strong and just as significant as their relationships with other humans. Yet today, as in over 100 years ago, individuals continue to struggle to find the appropriate outlet to express their pain, hiding heartache for fear of the social repercussions that might come with public acknowledgment of the existence of such a bond.

The RSPCA reassures the public on its website that they should not feel shame for their grief. In the UK, charities like the Blue Cross and Rainbow Bridge Pet Loss Grief Center offer counseling to bereaved humans.

Close relationships between people and animals have existed for millennia, but in western European cultures, there were few acceptable ways to mourn that relationship. As society becomes more accepting of the importance of human-animal relationships to our collective wellbeing, it is not surprising to see us follow rituals resembling those we use to mourn the loss of our closest human relationships.

At an estimated cost of €200 ($217) per service at the new Barcelona cemetery, it is important to acknowledge that this opportunity to grieve will not be financially available to everyone in the city.

This will not be a space for all of the city’s pets. Pet owners may opt to keep cremated remains within their home or spread out ashes in a meaningful location instead. Online forums and digital pet cemeteries also provide other opportunities to commemorate the relationship and express grief.

Whether one chooses a pet cemetery or not, there are many acceptable ways to express your grief – and to remember your relationship with the important animals in your life.

Influencers are now able to link their Amazon and Instagram accounts to promote products. Some are concerned about what they’re opting in to.﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

For years, influencers have come up with workarounds on social media to figure out how to share affiliate links with followers. A new integration between Instagram and Amazon was announced earlier this month as a way to make it easier for influencers to make money from affiliate links — but some content creators are suspicious about who really benefits.

The new integration allows creators to connect their Instagram and Amazon accounts and automatically tag products with their affiliate links, from which they earn a commission when followers make purchases. Influencers will be able to embed up to 30 product links in a Reel or 20 in a feed post, but a permissions setting has led to concerns about what creators are actually agreeing to.

In connecting an Amazon account, creators must agree to allow the retailer and its brand sellers to create ads from “any public content” that includes a related affiliate link. Influencers must also agree to acknowledge that brands can edit their content and use their “testimonial, caption or media” for ads.

The wide-ranging permissions are giving creators pause. Some have urged peers not to connect their accounts without reviewing the permissions and understanding how the feature would affect earnings. People making money on social media spend years tweaking their content and strategy to maximize reach, engagement, and, by extension, their bottom line. For some, it appeared that they would be giving Amazon and its sellers the ability to use their content under unclear terms. On Instagram head Adam Mosseri’s post announcing the feature, influencers complained about the lack of clarity, questioned whether using the feature would decrease their reach (which some creators say happens when they link to outside products), and demanded answers to whether their commission rate would stay the same when Amazon or brands use their content for ads.

Linking products through the new integration won’t reduce reach, Jimmy O’Keefe, Instagram’s director of product marketing, said in an email to The Verge. O’Keefe also noted that creators will continue to earn commission through affiliate links when Amazon boosts their posts, and that they can stop the boosting in settings or disconnect the integration entirely. There’s also a separate, manual way to add products without linking accounts, if a creator wants to opt out of having their content made into ads.

Amazon has an enormous influencer program that reaches across social media platforms. It is so lucrative that some content creators are able to make a living almost exclusively by hawking products for sale on Amazon, building empires on the shopping habits of their followers. When it comes to putting those links in front of followers, though, social platforms have historically been a roadblock, hence the cottage industry of link-in-bio tools meant to circumvent limits. Slowly but surely, though, platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and YouTube — perhaps chasing the success of TikTok Shop — have added more and more shopping features. The result is that shopping and social media begin to feel more and more like the same thing.

#236. Israel delays building contracts for West Bank settlement after UK sanctions

Attorney general says E1 settlement decision should not be taken by caretaker government led by Netanyahu

Israel has postponed issuing contracts for the construction of a large settlement on the West Bank seen as likely to render a two-state solution unviable, days after the UK imposed sanctions against building firms operating in the area.

Israeli diplomats insisted the move was not in response to the measures from Downing Street. Gali Baharav-Miara, the attorney general, said any decision on settlement expansion should not be taken by the caretaker government led by Benjamin Netanyahu but by whatever new administration was formed.

She ordered the Israel land authority and ministry of housing not to open the tender process. Israeli diplomats suggested the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, had acted prematurely on Monday in sanctioning the eight construction firms. But UK diplomats believe the growing political pressure on Israel over settlements, including from US Democrats, is having an impact.

The deferral puts the E1 settlement expansion in the mix for any coalition negotiations. The leader of the Change bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, seen as Israel’s most likely next prime minister, has been clear in opposing violent settler activity, as has the newly elected Knesset speaker, Matan Kahana, an ally of Eisenkot.

Eisenkot has also opposed the E1 settlement expansion, describing it as a mistake likely to alienate international opinion. He said of the plan: “I recall that Netanyahu himself opposed this for a long time, and due to coalition pressure, he gave in and approved it.”

The EI settlement expansion, due to have been announced on Thursday, has long been seen as qualitatively different since the land – between Jerusalem and Ma’aleh Adumim, a West Bank settlement city of nearly 40,000 residents – bisects the West Bank and cuts it off from East Jerusalem.

Miliband has said it would mark the death knell of a future Palestinian state. The UK, along with a group of European countries, has recently recognised Palestine, and the preservation of a two-state solution has been described as the north star of Labour policy towards the region.

The construction tender was published for more than 3,401 housing units in the area. At the beginning of November, the Israel Defense Forces began demolishing homes in a Bedouin community within the E1 area.

Israel has already enforced the downgrading of the UK consulate in East Jerusalem as a reprisal for Miliband’s decision in September to try to end trade links with the illegal settlements.

Although the Israeli election was largely fought on domestic security-related issues, Eisenkot seems to be more sensitive to the implications of Israel’s crumbling global reputation, and the need to make efforts to be seen to be listening to the criticism.

If he becomes prime minister, Eisenkot will, indirectly at least, also have to take account of the views of the Arab parties even if these parties are not going to become members of the government.

Valve announced some updates about Steam Machine availability today, including good news if you want to buy one right now and potential bad news about future supply due to RAMaggedon.

The good news: You can now purchase a 512GB Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist. Initially, interested buyers had to get on Valve’s waitlist if they wanted to purchase one, but the console-like PC is now available in an “add-to-cart” status, according to the company. As I write this, the 512GB versions with and without a bundled controller are showing estimated delivery dates of three to five business days on Valve’s website. If Valve sells through its current inventory, the company says it will indicate that the product is out of stock instead of making another waitlist.

The bad news: If you’re on the waitlist for a 2TB model, you might not get a chance to buy one at all, as Valve says there are more people on the waitlist than there are units available. The company is closing the waitlists for its 2TB models.

Valve says that while it’s still building more Steam machines, “memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels” and that it doesn’t know the number it can make or “at what price we’ll be able to offer them.” The 2TB Steam Machine is “especially constrained.” The company anticipates “having more information” to share about additional supply in January.

After delaying the Steam Machine’s expected early 2026 launch due to the memory and storage crisis, Valve launched the product in June with a price starting at $1,049 for the 512GB model without a bundled controller. A 2TB model without a controller costs $1,349.

#233. European leaders present united front in push for peace in Ukraine

Talks in Berlin end with reaffirmed support for Kyiv and a concerted push for European representation at future peace talks to end Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Below, you can review the top news from the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin on Thursday, 19th November, below:

Ukraine and three of its key European allies have reiterated their commitment "towards a comprehensive, just and lasting peace for Ukraine," which they described as being "vital for the security of Europe."

In a joint statement issued after Coalition of the Willing talks in Berlin, the leaders of Germany, France, the UK and Ukraine condemned  Russia's "systematic escalation of its deliberate and indiscriminate missile and drone attacks against Ukraine's civilians and civilian infrastructure."

Ukraine's right to defend itself was highlighted, as were Russia's battlefield losses.

The four leaders condemned "Russian hybrid attacks across Europe" and said they "would increase their resolve to strengthen the defence of Ukraine, Europe and NATO."

Leaders pledged "long-term and comprehensive support" for Kyiv and said that Ukraineäs air defense capability was a priority.

Russia's funding of its war effort would be targeted through sanctions and "pressure on Russian oil and gas revenues," while efforts to impede Russia's shadow fleet would continue.

On Ukraine's security, the leaders said the country needed "robust and legally binding security guarantees in place, once a ceasefire enters into force."

The statement mentioned "a European-led Multinational Force Ukraine composed of contributions from willing nations and supported by the US," something that has proven to be a sticking point for Russia.

The leaders said they supported "direct dialogue" between Kyiv and Moscow with US and European participation.

Ukraine's right to choose its own security arrangements needed to be "fully respected," the joint statement said.

"As a first step towards a cessation of hostilities, the leaders called on Russia to agree to an energy ceasefire for the duration of the winter," the statement read.

US special envoy Jared Kushner said unity in Europe was clear in the talks and that support for Ukraine remained strong.

"What we came away from today with is really seeing that Europe is very united and very, very strong in their support of Ukraine," Kushner said. "We relayed this to President Trump."

Kushner said this would also be relayed to the Russian delegation and that there was "a real desire for peace."

Kushner said that Trump had joined the Berlin meeting by phone and provided an update on the talks in Shenzhen with President Putin and President Xi.

"He sent a very strong message to both of them on the desire for peace and would like to engage with both of them very aggressively to get there," Kushner said.

Kushner told reporters the talks with European leaders ⁠and ​Ukrainian President ​Volodymyr Zelenskyy had "made a lot ​of progress ‌on what those security ​guarantees ⁠can look like," as well ⁠as ​a post-war prosperity plan.

He also said Russia was "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end the war.

French President Emmanuel Macron said that amid Russia's continued attacks on infrastructure and "maximalist demands," the first priority was for Ukraine to be able to defend itself.

Macron said allies needed to ensure that Ukraine had everything it needed to resist and defend itself from Russian attacks.

"Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine's accession to NATO," Macron said in Berlin.

"Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now," the French leader insisted, adding the priority was to deploy anti-missile systems and interceptors.

Macron said security guarantees were a "key element for our long-term negotiations" and the security plan it had already submitted should remain.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Europe should be part of talks going forward.

"America fully understands why strong and coordinated European participation at the negotiations is necessary," Zelenskyy said.

Zelenskyy said his country needed international support ahead of another winter and added that more work was needed to "push Russia to be more constructive in any negotiations."

He also said much work was done to make the Berlin meeting "as concrete as possible."

Zelenskyy thanked all partners and expressed gratitude to Germany, France, the UK, the US along with those who had come out in support of Ukraine.

Zelenskyy highlighted the importance of air defense and said that Russia's aerial bombardments were steadily intensifying.

Zelenskyy said there was no sign this would change as "the Russians have rejected every single proposal for de-escalation."

Zelenskyy said that it was "crucial" that the US "exerts influence on Russia."

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pushed for Europe to play a role in helping secure peace in the war in Ukraine.

"Today we prepared for ourselves for possible peace talks," Merz said.

"These talks should comprise Ukraine, Russia, the United States and Europe," Merz said, adding that this format offered the best chance of securing peace.

The German leader said Germany, France, the UK, Poland and Italy would speak on behalf of Europe.

He went on to call the trilateral talks between the president of the United States, Russia and China today at an APEC summit a "photo op" and said such a "Yalta format cannot bring peace" to Ukraine.

Merz pledged "powerful support" for Ukraine in 2027 and mentioned the €45 billion earmarked for next year by the European Commission.

Merz said the level of support was being provided in order for Ukraine to be able to protect itself and that allies wanted the war to end.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the future of European security would be molded by what was happening in Ukraine.

"The outcome of this war will shape security in Europe for a long time to come," Merz said in a post on social media platform X.

"Together with our partners, we continue our support for peace in Ukraine. That's why we came together today for the Coalition of the Willing," Merz said.

He accompanied his comments with pictures from roundtable talks of the "Coalition of the Willing" in Berlin.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he went over "key issues and needs" with German, French and British leaders.

Zelenskyy shared a video on X of his meeting with France's Emmanuel Macron, Britain's Andy Burnham and Germany's Friedrich Merz.

He said they discussed "countering Russian shahed drones and missiles, protecting the energy sector and infrastructure, as well as the diplomatic efforts."

"It is important that today's Coalition of the Willing meeting and bilateral meetings with leaders deliver results," he added.

Ukraine's European allies are gathering in Berlin in a show of support just hours after three-way talks took place involving the presidents of the US, Russia and China at the APEC summit.

European leaders are pushing to be included in US-backed talks to end the fighting in Ukraine with US special envoy Steve Witkoff and the US president's son-in-law Jared Kushner in Berlin for Thursday's meeting.

"Mr. Putin is not our friend and will never ​be," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said in a comment aimed at US President Donald Trump, who referred to Putin as "my friend" at a meeting on Wednesday.

"I find it very incomprehensible that a US president wants to sit down with President Putin," Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told ​reporters.

"I think Putin will be even more emboldened after today's meeting. He looks happy," she added. "Unfortunately, that is not a good sign for world ​peace. That is not ‌a good sign for Ukraine ... And therefore I think that what will come out of this is that he will hit us Europeans even harder, unfortunately."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised the EU was united in its support for Ukraine.

"Only through strength can we achieve a just and durable peace," she wrote on X. "We will maintain our support for Ukraine. And maintain full pressure on Russia. Europe stands strong and united."

Germany's push for more European aid for Ukraine is triggering a backlash.

Michaela Küfner discusses charges of "blackmail" against Chancellor Merz together with DW colleagues Nina Haase, Max Hofmann and Teri Schultz.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said that Moscow would not hold off on strikes in the Black Sea region or on energy infrastructure following strikes by Ukraine on the Kerch bridge.

The crucial road and railway crossing linking the Crimean peninsula with mainland Russia was put out of action by a series of Ukrainian strikes.

"But after the strikes on the Crimean Bridge, there will ⁠be no ​agreements. We will respond to these ​strikes. And I want everyone to know this: I believe ​our response will ‌be far more painful than what the Kyiv regime did to the bridge," he ​said.

Putin said ⁠the bridge was used exclusively for civilian purposes and not to ⁠transport military ​equipment, as Kyiv has alleged.

"We will, of course, restore the bridge. The road section suffered serious damage," Putin said.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said it would be unacceptable for there to be military cooperation between Ukraine and the EU, including any potential deployment of European troops to the country.

"Military cooperation in any form is, of course, a problem," Putin said at a press conference in China.

Putin also said European officials have been invited to Moscow to discuss the potential structure of talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.

"The American side is urging us to agree to the involvement of the Europeans ... Through diplomatic channels, we suggested to the Europeans to come to Moscow. And after that we will decide in what format the talks can continue," Putin told reporters.

"We understand that discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans," Putin added.

For months, European politicians have emphasized that they should be present at any talks on the future of Ukraine.

Leaders such as Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy, France's Emmanuel Macron, the UK's Andy Burnham, as well as US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived Thursday at the chancellery in Berlin for the talks.

The coalition is a grouping of countries that provide support to Ukraine against Russian aggression.

Leaders of Germany, France, Britain, Poland and Italy, as well as NATO head Mark Rutte and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will attend the meeting today.

The Ukrainian military on Thursday claimed responsibility for a strike on the Kerch Bridge.

The bridge was attacked on Wednesday for a third time this week, halting rail traffic briefly and damaging some sections.

In an online post, the Ukrainian military said that the strike had been carried out by its forces using Neptune coastal missiles.

It stated that the strikes on Russian bridges hamper Moscow's ability to transport military supplies to the front line.

The bridge, which supports a four-lane roadway and a railroad, is the only bridge linking mainland Russia with occupied Crimea.

"If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel," he said in an interview from Ukraine with The Telegraph.

Prince Harry, a former British Army officer and the younger son of King Charles III, traveled to Ukraine for his fourth visit since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, where he met with wounded veterans and medical staff.

Back in my day, the only “Doorbuster” sales were at physical retail stores. But now, you can get ultra-low prices before Black Friday whether you want to shop in-store or online. One that stands out is the previous-generation Sony WH-1000XM5 noise-canceling headphones, which are marked down to their lowest price ever, just $169.99 at Best Buy. While their MSRP is $399.99, they’ve been spotted as low as $198 in the last few months.

The WH-1000XM5 launched in 2022, and despite having been succeeded by the WH-1000XM6, they’re still an excellent set of headphones. Their active noise cancellation effect is one of the best out there — competitive with the latest models from Bose and Apple — and the sound profile is tighter and more balanced than the older Sony headphones. There are some minor downsides, like a bulky case and all-plastic design, but those seem easier to overlook at this lower price point.

The newer Sony WH-1000XM6 improve the sound and noise cancellation, with quality of life upgrades not present in the XM5, like a folding design and more comfortable headband. However, they’re significantly more expensive, currently discounted to $348 during Black Friday (Amazon, Best Buy), down from their MSRP of $450.

To make shopping a little more confusing, the newer WH-1000XM4C sit between the XM5 and XM6 in terms of price, and are a slightly updated version of the older XM4 model with its foldable design. Our reviewer John Higgins thinks the XM4C’s noise cancellation lags behind, so I’d opt for the XM5 over them, especially at the sale price.

#231. CEOs are tired of being held responsible for gun regulation

Americans have grown used to corporate executives treading the well-worn paths of the Northeast corridor to convene alongside elected officials in Washington, DC, and discuss geopolitics, policy and all that’s in-between.

In 2017, major CEOs from across the country came together to oppose North Carolina’s transgender bathroom law. In 2019, they called abortion bans “bad for business.”

After the deadly attack on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, many of corporate America’s biggest names denounced the rioters and pledged to halt their political giving.

Recently, more than 1,000 companies promised to voluntarily curtail their operations in Russia in protest of Moscow’s war on Ukraine.

Dick’s Sporting Goods stopped selling semi-automatic, assault-style rifles at stores and Citigroup put new restrictions on gun sales by business customers after the mass shooting at a high school in Parkland, Florida, in 2018.

A year later, after mass shootings at a Walmart in El Paso, Texas, and a nightclub in Dayton, Ohio, Walmart ended handgun ammunition sales.

Corporate leadership has long been vocal on the issue of gun control – in 2019 and again this past summer nearly 150 major companies – including Lululemon, Lyft, Bain Capital, Bloomberg LP, Permanente Medical Group and Unilever – called gun violence a “public health crisis” and demanded that the US Senate pass legislation to address it.

That’s why corporate America’s silence in the wake of the latest mass shooting at a school in Nashville is so jarring. The United States has come to rely on the increasing power of large corporations as political advocates.

But Yale professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a vocal advocate of corporate social responsibility who has a direct line to major CEOs around the globe, said that top executives are forlorn. Their previous efforts haven’t done much to push the needle on gun control legislation and without more backing, they don’t know what else they can do at the moment, he said.

Before the Bell spoke with Sonnenfeld, who runs Yale School of Management’s Chief Executive Leadership Institute, a nonprofit educational and research institute focused on CEO leadership and corporate governance.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Before the Bell: CEOs have been quiet about gun reform since the latest mass school shooting in Nashville, have you heard anything about plans to speak out?

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld: Where is everybody else? Where is all of civil society? CEOs are just one group of people and it’s like we’re turning to them to be our saviors on every topic. They’ve joined causes with valor and nobility but they can’t just be taking cause after cause as if there’s nobody else in society. The social change that happened in the 1960s wasn’t being led primarily by CEOs. Social changes really happened when we saw the interfaith activity of clergy locking arms and canvassing legislators. We saw campuses alive and aroused. Where’s all the student activism?

The CEOs are still the most active even if they’re less active than they were six months ago. They’re not there as hired hands of shareholders to fill the role of politicians and civic leaders. They’re there to join that chorus, but they don’t want to be the only one singing.

So is this what you’re hearing from top CEOs? Have they gotten tired of advocating?

I just got off of a CEO call on voting rights and this morning we had a forum on sustainability – CEOs are still the most active on these fronts. It’s the same thing on immigration reform. If a CEO was working an 18 hour day on a 12 day week, they still couldn’t address all of the issues that need addressing.

The nation’s CEOs are waiting for everybody else to join them. They don’t need to restate something they’ve already stated. They’ve jumped in the pool, where’s everybody else?

So what do you think has led to this complacency amongst Americans and the growing reliance on CEOs to advocate on our behalf?

They’ve taken a very strong stance and they’ve gone out further than the general public. They are where the general public is on surveys, but they’re not where the general public is on action in the streets. So we’re ready for others to now do something. Enough already on saying ‘what are the CEOs doing?’ Social capital is as valuable as financial capital. CEOs understand that in their soul, they want there to be social capital. They want there to be public trust, but they need the rest of civil society to join them. And that’s their frustration.

But don’t these CEOs hold the purse strings in terms of donating to powerful politicians?

You would think that, but since the 2020 elections much less of campaign contributions have come from big business. Since the 2021 run on the Capitol, a lot of businesses either had an official moratorium or they’ve given mere pennies to politicians. The common impression on the street that CEOs are controlling campaign purses strings is 100% wrong.

Tesla reported. a modest 4% rise in sales in the first quarter compared to the final three months of last year, despite a series of price cuts on its lower priced vehicles and talk by CEO Elon Musk about strong demand at those lower prices.

The first quarter also marked the fourth straight quarter that Tesla has produced more vehicles than it has delivered to customers. Some of that may be due to the ramp up in production at two new factories, one in Texas, the other in Germany, which opened last spring, and a lag between that increased production and sales.

Tesla said there was an increase in the number of its more expensive models, the Model S and Model X, in transit to Europe, the Middle East and Africa, as well as to the Asia Pacific region.

But it does mean that over the last 12 months Tesla has produced 78,000 more cars than it has sold, suggesting that talk of strong demand by Tesla executives may not be backed up by the numbers.

“Early this year, we had a price adjustment. After that, we actually generated a huge demand, more than we can produce, really,” said Tom Zhu, Tesla’s executive in charge of global production and sales. “And as Elon said, as long as you offer a product with value at affordable price, you don’t have to worry about demand.”

#229. FCC greenlights rule allowing prisons to jam cellphone signals

The FCC passed the rule despite warnings that jammers could block lawful communications, like 911 calls.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Federal Communications Commission voted unanimously to allow state and local prisons to jam cellphones. In an announcement on Thursday, the FCC argues the rule will help combat an “influx of contraband cellphones” used to carry out crimes from prison.

Jammers are generally banned under Section 333 of the Communications Act of 1934, though they’re used at some federal facilities. FCC Chair Brendan Carr claims that giving correctional facilities access to this technology will help prevent prisoners from using phones for illegal activity. “These devices [phones] are being used by inmates to order hits, run drug operations, traffic women and children, and unleash mayhem on our communities from behind bars,” Carr says.

In the months leading up to the vote, trade groups and human rights advocates have raised concerns about the risks of blocking cellphone signals in prisons. The US Chamber of Commerce and the CTIA, a wireless association representing the nation’s biggest carriers, have both warned in letters to the FCC that jamming technology could disrupt lawful communications outside prisons, including 911 calls. Meanwhile, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) has long argued that cellphones can keep prisoners safe by allowing them to document safety and human rights issues that the outside world may not see.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, the sole Democrat on the Commission, voted for the measure despite the risk of “potential unintended consequences,” according to the Associated Press. “I want to make sure that we don’t harm public safety in the name of helping public safety,” Gomez added.

The FCC says prisons that choose to jam cellphone signals will need to obtain a license, adhere to “technical standards and testing requirements,” and ensure that the jamming technology doesn’t interfere with communications outside the facility. Prisons must also notify nearby communities of testing and when the technology is being deployed.

#228. Eight injured after driver in Israel repeatedly rams car into Palestinians

Arab MPs accuse politicians of fuelling hostility as footage shows driver accelerating towards Palestinians at four locations in Kafr Qasim

Eight people were injured on Wednesday evening when a driver struck Palestinian residents at four separate locations in Kafr Qasim, a city in central Israel.

Footage shared on social media appears to show the car accelerating towards people, all Palestinians, at several locations in the city, striking them before driving away. Three of those injured were in moderate condition, and several of the victims were women leaving a nearby wedding, the Times of Israel reported.

Haaretz has reported that investigators are examining whether the driver struck people deliberately. Avi Levy, a police district commander, said the incident appeared to be a hit-and-run and that the driver had tested positive for drugs. He said the Shin Bet security service was taking part in the investigation and said: “As of this moment, nothing is coming up. The suspect has no criminal record.”

The incident prompted Arab lawmakers and activists to accuse Israeli politicians of fuelling hostility towards Arab citizens. Benjamin Netanyahu has called Arab parties “terror supporters” and said partnering with them would put Israel’s security at risk. The parties won a record 19 seats in the Knesset in the country’s recent election.

Yousef Jabareen, the chair of the Joint List, said the incident “raises difficult questions about the claim that the driver lost control”. He said: “I’ve been warning for weeks that the incitement against Arab citizens will turn into assaults and even assassinations.”

Said Issa, a community activist in Kafr Qasim, described the incident as an “act of terror”. “Someone who loses control of his vehicle might hit one or two vehicles, but not multiple people in several different places,” Issa said. “The attacker struck at four locations, one after the other.”

In a separate incident in the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian foreign ministry called on Monday for an Israeli settler to be held accountable after eight Palestinians were run over and injured in Tuqu, south-east of Bethlehem. Local sources told the Anadolu news agency that the driver had first struck three young men, then returned and ran over five others who had gathered to help them.

#225. Israeli tanks cross ‘yellow line’ boundary into Hamas-controlled central Gaza

First incursion across boundary since ceasefire deal comes as Eisenkot seeks to form government without Netanyahu

The Israeli military crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza on Wednesday in its first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed last October, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.

Israeli tanks rolled along the Salah al-Din road, Gaza’s main north-south route, a day after the US-backed Board of Peace, a body overseeing the ceasefire, accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities.

An Israeli military spokesperson said troops were carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of the yellow line in central Gaza.

The operation lasted about 24 hours and on Thursday the military said it had been “completed”.

The IDF ​has not commented extensively on the operation, which came as the Israeli opposition politician, Gadi Eisenkot, has been seeking to form a government without the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his political reputation on promises to keep Israel safe.

A Gaza security source told AFP there was “intense Israeli artillery shelling” north of Nuseirat refugee camp and reported Israeli military vehicles in central Gaza “amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes since midday”.

Hamas condemned the Israeli raid and the forced displacement of Palestinians as “a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement” and a dangerous escalation. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Hamas’s statement.

Residents reported hearing tank fire in the area. Palestinian medics said one person was killed in an Israeli airstrike near the site of the raid.

After the statement from the IDF that it had concluded the tank raid to dismantle a suspected Hamas tunnel, the defence ministry’s body in charge of civilian affairs in Palestinian territories, Cogat, said Palestinians would again be free to move in the targeted areas near al-Bureij and Nuseirat refugee camps.

In separate incidents on Wednesday, Palestinian medics said two people were killed by Israeli fire, one in Deir al-Balah and the other in Gaza City. The Israeli military said it was unaware of any incident in Deir al-Balah and had struck a militant in Gaza City.

Israel has stepped up its attacks on Hamas, which it says has been regrouping and rearming. Hamas has accused Israel of trying to derail the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025.

Israeli strikes have continued since the ceasefire, and Hamas remains armed.

Last week, an Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a surgeon and a disabled man, and wounded 28 others, according to the hospital director.

The body overseeing Donald Trump’s plan to end the war in Gaza has accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities, leaving Palestinians in dire conditions and the ceasefire at risk of collapse.

In its second report to the UN security council since the truce began 13 months ago, the Trump-led Board of Peace said the gap between what was agreed and what was happening on the ground remained the biggest threat to the deal. The report, seen by Reuters, warned that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely”.

Gaza’s health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire came into effect. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.

Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its military campaign in response to the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed.

In June, an ⁠independent UN inquiry determined that Israel was continuing to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children. A previous report by the commission in September 2025 found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, and Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited those acts. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) for war crimes.

Reuters and AFP contributed to this report

Google is updating its homepage to include AI searches. In a post on X, Google’s vice president of product, Robby Stein, shows how you can now open a collapsible sidebar to view and continue your AI chats.

Based on the GIF shared by Stein, it looks like you can open the sidebar by clicking the gray bar that appears on the left side of your screen. From there, Google will show a list of the searches you’ve made using AI Mode, along with the ability to start a new thread, search your threads, or connect a Gemini Notebook.

It’s yet another big change for Google’s homepage, which has long presented you with a single bar to kick off your web search. The company brought its AI Mode button to its search bar last year, which opens up a chatbot-like search experience within Google. In May, Google updated its search box to accommodate longer queries and added AI-powered autocomplete.

Stein says Google is rolling out the option because “people are coming to Search with more questions that aren’t just one and done,” adding that “in testing, this sidebar made a big difference for making progress & continuing to explore the web.” The new homepage is rolling out globally on desktop.

#222. Iraq's risky standoff: The state vs. Iran-allied militias

This week, Iraqi security forces surrounded an area run by the Kataib Hezbollah militia. Onlookers describe it as the most dangerous confrontation between the Iraqi state and Iran-allied militias in decades.

For years, there have all kinds of rumors about Jurf al-Sakhar, an area around 50 kilometers (31 miles) south of the Iraqi capital Baghdad. It is controlled by an Iraqi militia called Kataib Hezbollah, that's closely allied with Iran, and no Iraqi government troops or news media outlets have been allowed inside for around 12 years.

Rumors about what's happening in the area include allegations about secret prisons, mass graves, drone and weapons manufacturing and storage, as well as criminal activity such as oil smuggling. Jurf al-Sakhar is also allegedly a base for foreign, Hezbollah-supporting nationals from Iran, Yemen, Bahrain and Lebanon.

Recently two people —  an Israeli researcherand a US journalist — who were kidnapped by an Iraqi militia are thought to have been held captive in this area.

Jurf al-Sakhar previously had an estimated 89,000 residents but after the extremist group known as the "Islamic State," or IS, rose to power in Iraq in 2014, much of the population was displaced in fighting. The area was eventually taken over by Kataib Hezbollah, a militia that had fought IS alongside other armed groups.

As a collective, the armed groups are referred to as the Popular Mobilization Forces, or PMF. Not all of them have pledged allegiance to Iran but Kataib Hezbollah, a Shiite Muslim majority group, has.

In the past 12 years, tens of thousands of the displaced people from here, mostly Sunni Muslims, have not been allowed to return and the area has been described as militarized.

Its name was even changed by Kataib Hezbollah fighters, from Jurf al-Sakhar ("rocky bank") to Jurf al-Nasr ("bank of victory").

But recent events may shake Kataib Hezbollah's hold on this area.

An early November report for the Iraqi government says that since 2021, the group has smuggled hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil, siphoned from pipelines around Jurf al-Sakhar.

Iraq's new government, headed by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, made several arrests based on the report and demanded that Kataib Hezbollah leave Jurf al-Sakhar by Friday, Nov. 20.

Kataib Hezbollah rejected al-Zaidi's ultimatum, with a spokesperson saying the group would not withdraw "not even over our dead bodies."

Al-Zaidi then ordered state security forces to surround the area, while Hezbollah reportedly brought in reinforcements.

Observers have described the standoff as one of the most consequential and riskiest confrontations between an Iraqi government and Iranian-backed militiasin Iraq in more than two decades.

"It is a political signal that things will change, that he [al-Zaidi] wants to disarm militias, integrate them into state and claim back the state's authority," Ulf Laessing, head of the Syria and Iraq project for Germany's Konrad Adenauer Foundation, or KAS, told DW. "But it's a minefield and he needs to navigate carefully."

The standoff is also the result of long-running political tensions in Iraq, where the state is torn between its US allies on the one hand and Iranian allies on the other. Both hold sway in Iraq and are considered important relationships.

During Donald Trump's presidency of the US, and thanks to the US and Israel's war with Iran, there's been more pressure on Iraq to disarm Iran's allies inside the country. Al-Zaidi has set a deadline of next June to bring all weapons under the state's control.

The situation in Jurf al-Sakhar became even more tense this week. Al-Zaidi announced a new security plan for the area that involves other members of the PMF, state security forces and the police. Kataib Hezbollah rejected the plan.

"Al-Zaidi appears serious about ending Kataib Hezbollah's autonomous control of Jurf al-Sakhar," Hayder al-Shakeri, a research fellow at the British think tank Chatham House told DW. "Deploying federal forces and now establishing a new security command there shows this has moved beyond rhetoric."

But how dangerous is Kataib Hezbollah really? After all, al-Zaidi was actually nominated for the prime minister's job by a political bloc known as the Coalition Framework, or CF — these are the politicians who represent the PMF in parliament. Kataib Hezbollah's political party, Harakat Huqooq, is part of the CF.

And other researchers have been critical on social media, noting that the PMF troops that will be given partial control over Jurf al-Sakhar (should Kataib Hezbollah withdraw) are associated with that group anyway.

But Iraqi news media have also reported that there are divisions inside the CF, and apparently even within Kataib Hezbollah, about how to deal with the current standoff. Reportedly, some senior officials think that parts of Jurf al-Sakhar could be handed to federal forces in a gradual withdrawal, the London-based outlet Amwaj Media reported earlier this week, while some senior members of Kataib Hezbollah would seemingly prefer to hand the territory over to certain PMF brigades rather than to state security forces.

Late Thursday afternoon, the news agency Reuters reported that, according to three anonymous officials, all parties had come to an agreement that would allow government forces to enter Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday.

A compromise is good because it avoids violence, KAS' Laessing said. "It might not be what al-Zaidi initially hoped for but it's still a political signal."

If it did come to actual fighting, the Iraqi military has more resources than Kataib Hezbollah, al-Shakeri explained. "[It] could probably take Jurf al-Sakhar if the political leadership and security institutions remained united," he said. "But there would be no easy victory. Kataib Hezbollah does not need to defeat the Iraqi army conventionally. It can impose costs through asymmetric attacks, political pressure and its networks inside the state."

How the reported compromise plays out in the coming days, will also impact other Iraqi militias and they will be watching closely. Because "the core issue is whether a faction can continue controlling territory and economic activity beyond effective government oversight," al-Shakeri explained.

"The most likely compromise may be to remove Kataib Hezbollah's monopoly rather than remove the PMF from Jurf al-Sakhar altogether," he continued. "That would still matter if it opened the area to regular state forces, if it protects the oil infrastructure and places security under a clearer government command structure."

It could also lead to displaced residents being allowed back to their homes.

"But if one PMF faction simply replaces another while retaining its own networks and autonomy, then Zaidi has redistributed armed influence rather than fundamentally resolved the problem," al-Shakeri concluded.

#221. HSBC's top execs face tense shareholders calling for a breakup

HSBC’s top brass defended their strategy Monday to frustrated shareholders in the lender’s largest market, as Europe’s biggest bank continued to face calls to be split up.

At an informal shareholder meeting in Hong Kong, Chairman Mark Tucker and CEO Noel Quinn took questions from investors on issues ranging from how the bank was approaching demands for an overhaul of its business to its purchase of Silicon Valley Bank’s UK arm.

In prepared remarks, Tucker and Quinn each reiterated the board’s recommendation that shareholders vote against a resolution on the docket for its annual general meeting in May that would force the bank to come up with a plan to spin off or reorganize its Asian business — the lender’s main source of profits.

HSBC's biggest shareholder reignites debate about breaking up the bank

Tucker said the board was unanimous in its opposition to the resolution, stating plainly: “It would not be in your interest to split the bank.”

He said the board had previously reviewed a range of options for restructuring the bank, and concluded that such alternatives would “materially destroy value for shareholders,” including dividends.

“Our strategy is working,” Tucker told the room of more than 1,000 shareholders. “Our current strategy is moving dividends up.”

HSBC has been facing calls to separate its Asian business from the rest of the bank over the past year.

Shareholders in Hong Kong — where HSBC is a mainstay of many retail investors’ portfolios — contend that the London-based lender’s performance has been dragged down by its businesses in other regions.

Quinn addressed those complaints head-on Monday, saying “our profits in Hong Kong and the UK are no longer being dragged down by underperformance elsewhere. The group is performing well as a whole.”

Pressed later by a shareholder on the issue, Quinn said a breakup of the bank would result in “significant revenue loss” because much of its business relied on cross-border transactions.

Investors have also been unhappy with HSBC scrapping its dividend in 2020, at the request of British regulators. They argue that if the lender cordoned off its activities in Asia, it would no longer have to expose Hong Kong shareholders to requests in other jurisdictions.

Christine Fong, a district council member in Hong Kong, said she represented about 500 small shareholders who had been affected by the dividend cancellation.

“Street hawkers, taxi drivers or teachers — they all relied on the dividend to pay for their regular expenses, like mortgage, insurance payments, school fees,” Fong told CNN.

“That’s why, three years ago, what HSBC did upset those small minority shareholders.”

Fong has now joined calls for shareholders to vote in favor of the proposal for the bank to spin off its Asian business, despite the lender bringing back its dividend in 2021, albeit at a lower level.

Ken Lui, an activist shareholder in Hong Kong who put the resolution together, doubled down on his call for support ahead of the meeting Monday.

The resolution will require 75% of votes to be passed in May, but “nothing is impossible,” he told reporters outside the meeting venue.

Lui, who said he personally held a stake worth 100 million Hong Kong dollars ($12.7 million), laid out plans for his team to focus on “targeted outreach to institutional shareholders to present our case and gain their support.”

His group will also canvass 18 districts of Hong Kong “to tell HSBC shareholders that they finally have a chance to speak for themselves and protect their rights through voting,” he added.

HSBC is also facing pressure from its largest shareholder.

Ping An (PNGAY), China’s biggest insurer, holds an 8% stake in HSBC and has backed calls for the bank to rethink its structure.

In a series of remarks made public by the Chinese firm last November, Huang Yong, chairman of Ping An’s asset management arm, said “we will support any initiatives including a spinoff that are conducive to improve HSBC’s performance and value.”

Since then, the insurance giant’s views haven’t changed, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The source told CNN that Ping An has been calling for HSBC to explore a reorganization, with an eye on boosting its valuation and simplifying its regulatory obligations around the globe.

The insurer has not recommended a specific path forward but will support any initiatives, including a spinoff of its Asian business, that could boost its stock performance or value, the person added. Ping An did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how it planned to vote at the upcoming general meeting.

HSBC’s leaders were also asked Monfday why the bank had scooped up the British unit of SVB following the stunning collapse of its parent in the United States. The purchase was made for £1 ($1.20) last month, just days after SVB had folded.

Critics have questioned HSBC’s ability to perform adequate due diligence on SVB UK’s customers because of how quickly the deal came together.

“Did HSBC look into the clients of SVB in detail? Say, the financial statement — whether they can pay back the loan?” said Fong.

HSBC buys SVB's UK business, ending 'nightmare' for British tech

Quinn and Tucker defended the acquisition, calling it a good business opportunity that allowed the bank to gain hundreds of innovative startups as customers. They pushed back on the notion that management hadn’t had time to carry out proper due diligence.

Tucker also weighed in on recent tumult in the banking industry, saying he did not expect an “immediate impact” on HSBC.

“After the collapse of a number of smaller regional banks and the takeover of Credit Suisse, the share prices of all banks have been suppressed,” he noted.

But he said he did not believe such developments represented “a systemic risk” to the sector. “I do expect a period of uncertainty” before nerves settle, he added.

#219. Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel

Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent

The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.

In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.

The lengthy judgment will have been read particularly carefully by Israel, the only other country currently before the ICJ accused of genocide.

It is also relevant to Germany, which has been brought before the court by Nicaragua on the accusation it has facilitated and failed to prevent genocide in Gaza.

“I think it’s a judgment that brings the genocide convention alive,” said Philippe Sands, a leading human rights lawyer who was part of the Gambian legal team. “It gives the convention practical, real meaning. And if the alternative view had been taken, the convention would essentially become a dead letter.”

Amnesty International’s secretary general, Agnès Callamard, called the ruling “a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”. But it was also an assertion of humanitarian law in an increasingly lawless world.

“This is a good day for international law. We needed it,” said Dr Iva Vukušić, an assistant professor in international History at Utrecht University and a war crimes expert. “It is really important, clarifying a lot of law, and that’s going to be very helpful going forward.”

There will be a spillover from this ruling to its sister tribunal in The Hague, the international criminal court (ICC), providing a benchmark for when genocide charges could be made against individual perpetrators.

The Trump administration, instinctively hostile to international legal institutions, is also watching critically. The US ambassador to the UN told the ICJ before this judgment not to “lower the legal threshold for proving genocide” lest it be “weaponised” against US and allied soldiers.

The court did not directly lower the standard for demonstrating genocide, and the Gambia – which brought the case to The Hague – did not ask it to.

The judges kept the existing benchmark for judging genocide intent as the “only reasonable inference” of Myanmar’s actions and referred extensively to prior case law. But it went a long way towards clarifying how that standard should be applied in assessing atrocity crimes committed by states.

Before this case, only Serbia had faced the charge of genocide at the ICJ, in cases brought by Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Bosnian ruling in 2007, Belgrade was found to have failed to prevent the 1995 genocide in Srebrenica, but in both cases it was cleared of committing the genocide directly.

The new ICJ judgment finds the Myanmar military directly responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority targeted in a ferocious counterinsurgency campaign that reached its peak in 2017.

In assessing the Myanmar campaign, the ICJ looked not just at the death toll of about 10,000 in assessing the scale of the atrocities, but at the total Rohingya population targeted in northern Rakhine state, 815,000 people. Significantly, it cast its net wider than just the death toll, considering mental damage done to the survivors, particularly victims of sexual violence, and the impact on reproduction in the Rohingya community.

Most importantly, the ICJ judgment provided a guide to interpreting the standard set by Serbian cases, in which a finding of genocide could be made only if there were not other plausible motives for mass killing.

In this judgment, the court ruled that Myanmar could have had other motives, such as the desire to displace or punish the Rohingya population, but that those motives could exist alongside genocidal intent. The judges said genocidal intent was the “only reasonable inference” from the “totality” of evidence.

In justifying that conclusion the judges pointed to several factors that international law experts say are relevant to the Gaza case, which is now hearing written pleadings and is expected to take at least another three years.

The common factors include the targeting of children, which the court described as striking at the “foundation” of the Rohingya as a group – the ICJ said up to 2,109 Rohingya children under the age of five had been killed, while more than 5,000 Palestinian children under five years old have been killed in the Gaza war.

Another incriminating factor cited by the court was the “bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance” after the destruction of villages, followed by “rapid construction” including security installations, which has been the hallmark of Israeli army occupation of over 60% of the Gaza Strip.

“It’s full of messages for Israel,” said William Schabas, an international law professor and expert on genocide at Middlesex University. “There are obvious differences, of course, the evidence will be different, but if you exchanged the word Myanmar with Israel, you wouldn’t have to change much in the judgment.”

The fact that there were six dissenting voices on the bench suggested that substantial parts of the majority’s reasoning were not beyond dispute, and lawyers involved in the case cautioned that it did not necessarily mean that the same bench would find Israel guilty of genocide in Gaza. But the same lawyers added that the opposite was almost certainly true. If this case had failed, the case brought by South Africa against Israel would have been all but over.

#217. A brief history of Nvidia’s recent stock fluctuations

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Tracking the stock price amid Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs and alleged spy scandal.

Tracking the stock price amid Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs and alleged spy scandal.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

“We’ve got this,” Colette Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia, said Tuesday night as she closed out the embattled chip company’s third quarter earnings call.

By Thursday, the company’s stock price was hovering at around $150 per share, a nearly 40 percent drop from its all-time high on October 6th, and wiping out a brief post-earnings pop on Tuesday night. Meanwhile, Wall Street was paying up for one of Nvidia’s biggest customers as Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut at $111.50 per share — 34 percent higher than expected.

Looking at the earnings report numbers alone, Nvidia had a blockbuster quarter. Q3 revenue more than doubled from the same period last year up to total $115.8 billion, driven by data center revenue that was up 110 percent and exceeding Wall Street expectations. Nearly $20 billion in revenue came from the highly anticipated Vera Rubin platform, which shipped during the quarter, becoming the “fastest product ramp in company history,” Kress told investors.

“Our momentum is real,” Kress said. “With the market-leading multiyear roadmap, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade, and sustainable demand, we are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia’s leadership position.”

But investors are stilltrying to reconcile Nvidia’s stellar recent financial performance and position as a central pillar in the AI economy with serious concerns over its future.

The company’s stock has taken a stunning tumble in recent weeks. Fueled first by a broader market sell-off of chip stocks amid concerns about the AI bubble, the stock took another blow following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, according to US intelligence sources cited by The New York Times.

Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s newly appointed chairman of the board, told investors on the call Tuesday that the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and has already tapped an executive search firm to help find a replacement. Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has led the company ever since — famously without a succession plan — has become essentially inseparable from it in the eyes of Wall Street and the media. But while Huang may not be ready to let go, posting on X this week that he’d be “honored” to be reinstated as CEO, Nvidia’s executive suite seems ready to move on.

It has been a tumultuous two and a half weeks for Nvidia.

On October 29th, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies believed Jensen Huang to be the target of a Chinese espionage plot. The report centered on his “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company and one of Nvidia’s clients. Nvidia initially contested the report, adding that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang “are not unusual or unexpected.”

Nvidia’s stock seemingly remained unaffected by the reports, at least at first. The share price closed at $213.66 on October 29th, down just 0.8 percent from the previous day. (Julian Barnes, one of the reporters on the story, later commented, “I will confess I was kind of surprised that the world’s initial reaction to our October story was a bit muted.”) The stock closed at a 4 percent drop the next day as the entire Nasdaq fell 2.9 percent, the worst single-day decline since June.

The stock continued to fall through Wednesday, November 4th, the day after the blue wave swept the midterms, stoking fears on Wall Street that the new class of Democratic governors in key states like Texas would slow down data center construction. On Thursday, November 5th, Nvidia’s stock fell 9.2 percent, its largest single-day drop in at least a year. But chip stocks began to recover the next day, and by close on Friday, November 6th, Nvidia was back up 2.8 percent to a share price of $186.64.

Then all hell broke loose. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang sent a company-wide memo to Nvidia staff in which he apologized for engaging in an extramarital affair. The memo coincided with the opening of an independent investigation by Nvidia’s board into Huang’s alleged misconduct and whether company secrets or national security had been compromised. Huang said he would cooperate fully with the investigation. By the opening bell on Monday, November 9th, Nvidia shares had tumbled 7 percent and trading volume surged past its three-month average as investors reacted to the memo. After a brief rebound, the stock continued to oscillate the next day, as more details of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang’s relationship emerged. By the time the market closed on Tuesday, November 10th, Nvidia shares were down to $168.89, nearly 10 percent below the closing price on the last day of 2025.

The stock rebounded slightly on Wednesday, November 11th, as investors prepared for Nvidia’s third quarter earnings call, scheduled for the following Tuesday, November 17th. By Wednesday night, however, shares had plunged yet again as media reports circulated that Nvidia’s board was considering ousting Huang, and other reports emerged detailing a second alleged affair, this time between Huang and an Nvidia employee.

Nvidia announced Huang’s departure on the morning of Thursday, November 12th, sending the company’s shares falling nearly 14 percent at the open. It closed at just a 4.3 percent dip. The intraday low of $148.80 per share was its lowest price in a year.

On December 1st, Jensen Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee for transcribed interviews. Nvidia’s general counsel will do the same on December 2nd.

Retail investors have already seized the opportunity to buy the dip. In the first 30 minutes of trading on Thursday, November 12th, retail investors bought $111 million of Nvidia shares in the largest-ever first half-hour of opening for the stock, Bloomberg reported, citing Vanda Research.

Nvidia’s average price target is $232.59, with the lowest estimate at $130 and the highest at $350, according to an analysis of analyst projections over the last three months by Google Finance.

Nearly two-thirds of those analysts issued a “Buy” rating for Nvidia in the last three months. Of those, all 30 reiterated that rating post-earnings.

The stock closed at $145.98 on Thursday, a new 52-week low.

Then again, numbers are the core basis for stock market ratings, and numbers may not be Nvidia’s problem right now. It’s everything else — the leadership vacuum, upcoming congressional testimony, regulatory uncertainty, broader questions about neocloud customer financing and sales to China — that will continue to impact the stock in the coming weeks.

#216. China Renaissance suspends trading, delays results after founder's disappearance

China Renaissance, a top dealmaker in the country’s tech industry, said it would suspend trading of its shares and delay the release of its annual results because it still can’t get in touch with its founder.

Bao Fan, 52, started the boutique investment bank in 2005 and has been unreachable since the middle of February, according to the company. Shares in China Renaissance have plunged since Bao went missing, at one point dropping as much as 50%.

China Renaissance said in late February that it had learned Bao was “cooperating in an investigation” being carried out by certain authorities in the country. It gave no other details.

Chinese media have reported Bao might be assisting in an investigation related to a former executive at China Renaissance.

In a filing on Sunday, China Renaissance said auditors couldn’t complete their work or sign off on their report because of Bao’s absence. The board was also unable to give an estimate about when it would be able to approve its audited results for 2022 or dispatch its annual report by an April 30 deadline as required by Hong Kong’s listing rules.

Missing Chinese billionaire CEO assisting authorities in investigation, company says

Trading in the company’s shares was suspended from Monday as a result.

Bao is known as a veteran dealmaker who works closely with top technology companies in China. He helped broker the 2015 merger between two of the country’s leading food delivery services, Meituan and Dianping. Today, the combined company’s “super app” platform is ubiquitous in China.

His team has also invested in US-listed Chinese electric vehicle makers Nio (NIO) and Li Auto and helped Chinese internet giants Baidu (BIDU) and JD.com (JD) complete their secondary listings in Hong Kong.

Over the weekend, China’s top anti-graft watchdog launched an investigation into Liu Liange, former party secretary and chairman of Bank of China, according to a statement by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the State Supervision Commission. The bank is state-owned and one of the country’s four biggest lenders.

Liu is suspected of “serious violations of discipline and law,” the statement said. He is among the most senior financial executives targeted in a broader financial crackdown by President Xi Jinping.

In January, Wang Bin, former party chief and chairman of China Life Insurance, was charged by national-level prosecutors with taking bribes and hiding overseas savings.
